I can't speak for for all alternative (although I prefer the term "complementary") medicines, but as a student of traditional Chinese medicine I think it's worth pointing out that a lot of the methodology used in testing efficacy according to the western method often simply isn't valid when applied to other modalities.

In Chinese medicine, treatment is designed and applied on an individual-by-individual basis. We view diseases as having multiple possible causes which can become very complex and require very different treatments. Because of this, two patients who have been diagnosed with the same disease in western medical terms will often be treated by Chinese medicine in very different ways.

The current standard research model is based on the idea that groups of subjects with the same diagnosis, given the same treatment, should have the same result if the treatment is effective. But a Chinese medical practitioner would never treat people in this way; we would examine every individual patient, and give each of them a unique prescription to give them the best results. To us, giving all the patients the same treatment without proper examination and differentiation is basically malpractice.

Unfortunately a study in which every patient was treated differently would never be considered to be scientifically valid, so we have to treat patients in a way that isn't considered to be appropriate, and accept mediocre-at-best research results. I'm sure Chinese medicine isn't alone in this dilemma, so it's worth keeping an open mind about these things.

But not too open, you don't want your brain to fall out either.

Frankly, I don't think you understand how medical science works. The reason big medical studies sometimes include hundreds of thousands of subjects is to achieve the statistical resolution needed to tease out the influence of small "individual" differences. If a treatment works on one person but fails on another who received the same diagnosis, the Western approach to medicine is to try to understand why, not just shrug and move on.

I (my wife, actually) recently experienced a concrete example of this. She had a urinary tract infection. But because she is pregnant, her nurse midwife prescribed a different antibiotic to her than she ordinarily would in order to reduce the risk of harming the baby.

The real difference between Chinese and Western medicine is not that Western doctors don't treat patients as individuals. It's that Chinese medicine persists in treating patients based on philosophical principles, a practice the West largely jettisoned several hundred years ago when we gave up on the "four humours" in favor of empiricism.
